content: Th-fronting is a linguistic phenomenon where the dental fricatives /θ/ (as in three) and /ð/ (as in this) are replaced by labiodental fricatives /f/ and /v/, respectively. This sound change has occurred independently in various English dialects, including Cockney, Newfoundland English, African American Vernacular English (AAVE), and Liberian English. However, the specifics of how this change manifests differ across these accents. In accents where th-fronting occurs, words like three and free, slither and sliver, or oath and oaf become homophones. Despite this, speakers of these accents generally retain an awareness of which words are traditionally associated with which sounds. In many cases, the two sounds appear in free variation, meaning they can be used interchangeably without altering the meaning of the word. Th-fronting does not occur at the beginning of words for the voiced dental fricative /ð/ (as in this). Instead, it is observed intervocalically (between vowels) or at the end of words. For example, the word brother might be pronounced with a /v/ sound instead of /ð/, and with might end with an /f/ sound. This feature is famously associated with the Cockney accent, where the labiodental fricatives /f/ and /v/ replace the dental fricatives /θ/ and /ð/. Th-fronting has also been noted as spreading to other non-standard accents in England. According to linguist Peter Trudgill, this change has been observed in working-class speech and is slowly making its way into middle-class accents, including Estuary English. Estuary English is a variety of English spoken in the southeast of England, and th-fronting serves as a boundary marker distinguishing Cockney from Estuary English. However, phonetic studies, such as those conducted by Ulrike Altendorf, have shown that th-fronting occasionally appears in middle-class Estuary English speech as well, suggesting that it is gradually becoming more widespread. An example of th-fronting in Cockney speech can be found in a recording of a speaker describing their family background: My dad came from Wapping and me mum came from Poplar. Me dad was one of eleven kids… and Wapping in them days really was one of the poorest parts of London. I mean they really didn’t have shoes on their feet. I’m talking about seventy years ago now… and Poplar was… just slightly a cut above Wapping; erm… you was either East End respectable or you was sort of East End villain, you know, and my family was respectable on both sides.” In this recording, words like father and brother are pronounced with /v/ instead of /ð/, and Thursday is pronounced with /f/ instead of /θ/. Th-fronting has been spreading in Southern England, albeit at a slower rate compared to other phonetic changes like t-glottalization (the replacement of /t/ with a glottal stop). Interestingly, th-fronting has also been reported in the speech of working-class adolescents in Glasgow, Scotland, as of 1998. This finding sparked both academic and general interest, as it challenges traditional models of language change that rely on dialect contact and geographical mobility. The Glaswegian speakers who exhibited th-fronting in the 1997 sample were found to have the lowest levels of geographical mobility, raising questions about how this feature spread in a relatively isolated linguistic community.
